title: Buying Your Business Premises: Will the Building Still Work in Five Years?
excerpt: The right commercial property must do more than fit your business on inspection day. Test its operational suitability, adaptability and ownership demands before treating it as your long-term home.
metaTitle: Buying Business Premises: The Five-Year Fit Test | YOS
metaDescription: A practical commercial property suitability checklist for NSW owner-occupiers, covering growth, access, adaptability and ownership responsibilities.
body:
## How do you know a commercial property will suit your business long term?

Test it against how you operate today, a realistic growth scenario and a slower trading scenario. Confirm that the intended use, access, layout and building services can support those needs, then assess the ownership costs and constraints with the appropriate advisers.

Five years is a planning horizon for this exercise, not a forecast of property values or your business performance. The purpose is to expose assumptions while you can still investigate them.

## Write an owner-occupier brief before inspecting

List what the business requires from its premises: staff capacity, customer access, storage, deliveries, private rooms, equipment and utilities. Mark each requirement as essential or desirable and note the evidence needed to verify it.

For example, 'space for more staff' is vague. 'A measured layout that accommodates additional workstations without removing the meeting room' is something you can test with a designer.

## Try three versions of your business

| Scenario | Question to test | Evidence to obtain |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Current operations | Can the site support a normal busy day? | Measured layout, access checks and services information |
| Growth | Can we add people, equipment or a service line? | Concept layout and advice on alterations and approvals |
| Slower trading | What commitments remain if revenue falls? | Ownership cost schedule and finance scenarios from advisers |

Do not assume spare floor area equals usable capacity. Circulation, amenities, storage, access and services may limit what the building can accommodate.

## Look beyond the property boundary

Visit at relevant operating times. Check how customers arrive, how deliveries reach the site and whether nearby parking or transport is suitable. Distinguish parking you own or have documented rights to use from parking that simply happened to be available during an inspection.

Ask a qualified adviser to investigate intended use, zoning, approvals and restrictions. For strata property, request the relevant records and advice about common property, rules, maintenance obligations and proposed expenditure. These are investigations, not matters to assume from a listing description.

## Test adaptability before budgeting a transformation

A building may look adaptable while requiring substantial changes to services or access. Have the appropriate professionals assess what the proposed use and alterations require, including landlord or strata involvement where relevant and the approvals pathway.

Furniture planning and client-side FitOut advice can help test your operational brief before the purchase decision. They complement building, planning and legal investigations; they do not replace them.

## Make the ownership workload visible

Create a schedule of recurring costs, likely maintenance, immediate works, insurance and professional fees. Have your accountant, solicitor and finance adviser assess the tax, ownership structure, transaction and borrowing implications for your circumstances.

Keep purchase price, fitout expenditure and working capital separate. Avoid allocating every available dollar to the purchase and discovering that the business cannot fund the changes needed to operate there.

## Use an evidence register before committing

For each essential requirement, record the answer, its source, any remaining question and who will resolve it. An unresolved critical item should prompt investigation or appropriate contractual advice, rather than an optimistic tick.

A commercial buyers agent can help refine the acquisition brief, source and compare properties, coordinate enquiries and negotiate the purchase. Independent professional advice remains necessary for legal, financial and technical matters.

## Questions business owners ask

### Does buying premises guarantee more stability?

Ownership can give a business greater control, but introduces finance, maintenance and capital commitments. Whether that trade-off suits you depends on the property and your circumstances.

### Can I assume I can expand or change the use later?

No. Investigate the relevant controls, building constraints and approvals with suitable professionals before relying on a future change.

### What should I prepare for a buyers agent?

Bring your operational brief, preferred locations, timeframe and adviser-confirmed budget parameters. Include both immediate requirements and the changes you expect the premises to accommodate.
